newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian lingerie firm limbers up for listing.
newsitem.headline: Belgian lingerie firm limbers up for listing.

text.p: Fancy slipping into something comfortable this September?
Belgian lingerie maker Van de Velde Gebroeders NV -- better-known by its Marie Jo, Prima Donna and L'Aventure brands -- hopes so.
The Ghent-based company plans an initial public offering on the Brussels Stock Exchange of up to 40 percent of its capital.
"That is the absolute maximum. We want to keep control of the company. Normally, it will be around 35 percent," Herman Van de Velde, one of three managing directors, told Reuters.
Founded in 1919 as a corset maker, the firm, owned by Belgium's Van de Velde and Laureys families, has built up a sizeable empire in luxury and fashionable ladies underwear.

From sales of just 110 million francs in 1973, the company now boasts turnover of more than 1.8 billion francs and employs 790 people in Belgium, Hungary and Tunisia. About 40 percent of production comes from subcontractors in China.
Van de Velde said the company's net margin was around 11 percent of sales in 1996 and 1997 was looking better.
"Sales rose 16 percent in the first half," he said. "July is already much higher than last year and the margin is increasing."
The stock market listing was essential for the company to maintain momentum and a lean management structure, he said.
"The third generation of shareholders are all active in the company. In the fourth generation there will be 18 shareholders and we have to organise things. A listing allows this," he said.
He said it was too early to comment on the likely pricing of the offering, but there were no plans to use it to raise fresh capital by issuing new shares.
The company is at present represented by 2.6 million shares.
The offering is led by Belgian brokerage KB Securities . Co-managers are CERA Investment Bank (formerly Bank Indosuez Belgium) and Bank Brussels Lambert.
A KB Securities spokesman said the listing would probably take place in the first half of September.
Van de Velde said the opportunity a listing created for raising fresh capital in the future was another reason the company had decided to go to the market.
"For example, at the moment we are not working in distribution. The company could one day do that," he said.

The firm at present sells its wares exclusively through a network of 4,000 private outlets in Europe. Belgium accounts for 24 percent of sales, neighbouring European countries for 58 percent and other European states for 16 percent.
Only two percent goes to markets outside Europe and the company has no plans to change that, Van de Velde said.

"We are a European company and we think we have enough potential in Europe...especially Germany and France. Maybe if opportunities arise in the Far East or the U.S., where we already export, we would take them but it's not our priority."
